To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) the presence of adsorbed inorganic species on the surface of TiO2 can significantly reduce its photoactivity; (ii) the reduction in photoactivity is caused by the adsorbed species capturing photogenerated electrons and/or reducing adsorption of the organic pollutants; (iii) the adsorbed phosphate can reduce the photoactivity by capturing photogenerated electrons; (iv) in the case of adsorbed alumina, the reduction in photoacivity is caused by the formation

the adsorption of hydrous oxo-metal species onto TiO2 can reduce photocatalytic reactivity by suppressing charge transfer and/or reducing the adsorption of organic reactants, as well as by reducing the photogreying of the TiO2.
the photocatalytic oxidation and reduction of organic compounds and the photogreying of TiO2 can be significantly inhibited by surface adsorbed inorganic ions, such as Al3+ and Si4+.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the influence of naturally occurring inorganic species on photocatalysis.
the influence of surface inorganics on the photocatalytic degradation of organic pollutants.
the influence of naturally occurring inorganics on photocatalytic oxidation, and with the influence of inorganics on the photogreying of titanium dioxide.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
inorganic surface deposits reduce the photoactivity of TiO2.
inorganic species, including phosphate and silica, reduce photocatalytic activity.
the photocatalytic oxidation and reduction reactions are significantly suppressed by adsorbed inorganic species.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the presence of inorganic species in the water can have a significant effect on the photoactivity of the TiO2 surface, which can be detrimental or beneficial, depending on the chemical species and the reaction.
the presence of other species, especially inorganic species, can significantly reduce photocatalytic activity, and that these reductions can be quantified.
the presence of inorganics in water reduces the activity of the TiO2 photocatalyst by reducing adsorption, charge transfer and photogreying.
The main takeaway from our work is that
practical photocatalytic applications must be designed to take into account the effects of naturally occurring inorganic species in the water.
the surface of TiO2 is not a passive substrate, and that the presence of inorganic adsorbed species may be a significant factor in determining its photoactivity.
the presence of inorganic species on the surface of TiO2 photocatalysts will reduce photocatalytic degradation.
